subject: business-studies
title: Break-even Stretch Adventure
welcome_lead: Exam-style stretch. Evaluate changes to price, costs and use a break-even chart correctly.
meta_desc: GCSE Business Studies stretch — analysing changes to price/costs and reading break-even charts.
final_note: You can analyse how price and cost changes shift the break-even point and read a chart.

walkthroughs.body_html:
The break-even point is where the total revenue line crosses the total cost line.

Output on x-axis, money on y-axis. Below the cross = loss; above = profit.

Raise the price → contribution rises → break-even FALLS.

Raise fixed costs → break-even RISES. Raise variable cost → contribution shrinks → break-even RISES.

Quote the numbers, calculate the NEW break-even, then evaluate impact on profit and risk.

Discuss assumptions: prices, costs and demand may not actually behave like the model.

options: Falls
Rises
Stays the same
Doubles

mcqs.q: Which appears on the X-AXIS of a break-even chart?
options: Money
Output (units)
Profit
Fixed costs
Break-even is where the business owes no debt.
Break-even is where the business makes the most profit.
The level of output where total revenue equals total costs — neither profit nor loss. It is NOT the level where profit is maximised; profit grows beyond break-even.
Profit is what businesses earn; revenue is what employees earn.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between fixed and variable costs?
options: Fixed costs do not change with output level (e.g. rent, salaries); variable costs change in proportion to output (e.g. raw materials, hourly wages).
Fixed costs are paid every month and variable costs are paid weekly.
Fixed costs are the cheapest costs and variable costs are the most expensive.
Break-even is where the business owes no debt.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between profit and revenue?
options: Break-even is where the business owes no debt.
Profit and revenue are different words for the same thing.
Profit is what businesses earn; revenue is what employees earn.
Revenue is total income from sales (price x quantity sold); profit is revenue minus total costs — what is left after paying for everything.
